For example, in the United States, the General Social Survey found the share of adults saying “most people can be trusted” fell from 46% in 1972 to 34% in 2018, and a 2023–24 Pew survey found the figure remained at 34% .
This suggests a decades-long decline in social trust (especially from the 1970s to 1990s), with levels plateauing at historically low levels in recent years.

Globally, an Ipsos poll (Feb–Mar 2022, 22,534 adults in 30 countries) found that on average only 30% of adults agreed that “most people can be trusted.” However, interpersonal trust varies widely by country, from around 56% in China and India to under 15% in Brazil, Malaysia, and Turkey .

A global study led by the University of Melbourne and KPMG (surveying 48,000 people across 47 countries in late 2024) found that while 66% of people use AI regularly, only 46% are willing to trust AI systems .

Moreover, comparisons to earlier data show a decline in trust coinciding with the rise of generative AI in 2022: in the 17 countries surveyed before ChatGPT’s release, the share of people willing to trust AI fell from about 63% in 2022 to 56% in 2023 , accompanied by a jump in concern about AI’s risks (the proportion “worried about AI” rose from ~49% to 62% over that period) .

The KPMG-Melbourne survey revealed a “clear split” between emerging and advanced economies: roughly three in five people (60%) in emerging economies say they trust AI, compared to only two in five (40%) in advanced economies .

In short, trust in AI systems themselves does not appear to be rising with AI’s popularity – if anything, global trust in AI has declined since late 2022 (category b), and public confidence in AI’s use remains much lower for sensitive tasks, especially among publics in advanced economies.

The Reuters Institute Digital News Report 2023 – based on a massive survey of 93,000 online news consumers across 46 countries – found that only 40% of people on average said they trust “most news, most of the time,” down 2 percentage points from the previous year .
This modest decline in 2022–23 effectively reversed the temporary rise in media trust seen during the COVID-19 pandemic, resuming a prior decades-long slide .

adults), only 31% of Americans have a “great deal or fair amount” of confidence in the mass media, essentially tied with the record low of 32% first recorded in 2016 .
By contrast, in the early 1970s roughly 70% of Americans trusted the media – illustrating a precipitous long-run decline.
Notably, for the third year in a row, more Americans say they have no trust at all in the media (36%) than say they have at least a fair amount of trust (31%) .
The recent 2-point dip in global news trust from 2022–23 is consistent with pre-existing trends (category a) rather than a sudden acceleration due solely to AI.

Surveys show the public is highly aware and worried: in an August 2023 YouGov poll of Americans, 85% said they were “very” or “somewhat” concerned about the spread of misleading “deepfake” videos and audio .

A 2024 study in American Political Science Review simulated scenarios of politicians invoking “fake news” or “deepfake” claims to dodge scandals – a prime example of the liar’s dividend tactic – and found that these false claims helped politicians shore up support among their base, but did not significantly reduce overall trust in media .

The OECD’s 2023 cross-national Trust Survey (nearly 60,000 people in 30 countries) reports that on average just 39% of citizens had “high or moderate” trust in their national government in 2023, down slightly from 43% in 2021 .
In the U.S., for instance, public trust in the federal government to “do the right thing” most of the time fell from ~73% in 1958 to around 20% in recent years .
By June 2023, only 16% of Americans said they trust the government in Washington almost always or most of the time, one of the lowest levels in seven decades of surveys .
A 2025 study analyzing thousands of surveys since 1958 concluded that “globally, trust in representative institutions has generally been declining in recent decades” .

Key upcoming events, like the 2024–2026 election cycles in various countries, have fueled speculation that AI-generated fake news or bogus videos could accelerate the erosion of trust in leaders and democratic processes (potentially a category b scenario if it occurs).
The 2023 Edelman “Trust at Work” report found a “stunning” 23-point higher trust in “My Employer” compared to societal institutions overall among employees (23-point above the general trust index) .

Microsoft’s 2022 Work Trend Index (20,000 people in 11 countries) highlighted “productivity paranoia,” with 85% of business leaders saying the shift to hybrid work made it challenging to trust that employees are productive .

Where a short-term shift has been observed – such as the drop in global AI trust from 2022 to 2023 – it remains challenging to distinguish whether this is an effect of AI’s arrival or part of normal opinion variation.

The 2024 APSR experiment found no overall decrease in media trust when subjects were told a real political video was a deepfake , suggesting the liar’s dividend may not be as potent in practice as many fear.
